blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Today we go back to Australia. We will visit a lake, a sausage sizzle and a famous horse race. We will also learn some work rules that surprise visitors.

items.prompt: What do you like to do on a Saturday?
Do people in your country stop work to watch a sport?
Do you leave a tip in restaurants?

blocks.title: Part 1: A Lake in the Middle of Canberra
paragraphs: Canberra is the capital of Australia, and it is a **planned city**. People drew the city on paper first, and then they built it.
Why? When Australia became one country, **Sydney and Melbourne both wanted to be the capital**. They could not agree. So the government built a new city between them.
Two Americans, a husband and wife, won a competition to draw the new city. They were Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin. **For the Griffins, a lake was the heart of the city.**
Why a lake? The river was in low land between hills. **Water could fill this low land easily and cheaply, and a lake would be beautiful.** So the Griffins drew the city around it.
But Canberra had only a small river. So workers built a **dam**, a big wall that stops a river. In 1963, they closed its gates. **The river water stopped at the wall, and slowly it made a lake.**
Its name is Lake Burley Griffin. Today **the lake is the weekend park for the city**.

- People walk or ride bikes on the bridge-to-bridge loop. It is a 5-kilometre circle. It goes over two bridges.
- Rowing clubs train in long, thin boats at the west end.
- Families cook lunch on the free electric barbecues by the water.

blocks.title: Part 2: The Sausage Sizzle and Election Day
paragraphs: A **sausage sizzle** is a barbecue that sells food to raise money for a group. Sizzle is the sound of food cooking on a hot plate. You get one sausage in a slice of white bread. Many people add fried onions and tomato sauce.

The most famous ones are outside Bunnings, a big hardware shop. A hardware shop sells tools and things for your house and garden. On weekends, a local group, like a school or a sports club, cooks there.
**Bunnings takes no money from the group, so the group keeps it all.** A sausage costs $3.50.
Sausage sizzles also appear on **election day**, the day people vote. They are at polling places, the places where people vote. Why there?

In Australia, **voting is compulsory**. Every Australian citizen aged 18 or older must vote. People who do not vote can get a fine. A fine is money you pay when you break a rule. Because of this law, more than 90% of people vote in national elections.

Elections are on Saturdays, and people often vote in schools. **Almost everyone comes, so school parents cook for the long lines.** The money helps the school. Australians call this a **democracy sausage**. In a democracy, people choose their leaders by voting.

blocks.title: Part 3: The Melbourne Cup
paragraphs: The **Melbourne Cup** is the most famous horse race in Australia. In a **race**, horses run to see who is fastest. People call this one **the race that stops a nation**. For a few minutes, almost all of Australia stops to watch.

- When: the first Tuesday in November, at 3 pm
- Where: Flemington Racecourse in Melbourne
- How long: 3,200 metres

Why does all of Australia stop for one race? **Cup Day is a public holiday in Victoria**, the state where Melbourne is. People there do not go to work. They go to the race, or they watch it on TV with friends.
In other states, Cup Day is a normal work day. But **many offices stop at 3 pm.** People watch the race together on TV.
Many offices also have a **sweep**. It is a small game for the race.

- Everyone pays the same, often a few dollars.
- Each person takes a horse's name from a hat.
- The person with the winning horse gets about half of the money.
**You do not need to know about horses.** It is all luck, so everyone in the office has a horse to cheer for.
In 2026, a horse called **Point Of Law** won. Its **trainer** was Ciaron Maher. A trainer gets a horse ready for races. Ciaron Maher also trained the horses in second and third place.
**This was the first time in 166 races. One trainer had the first three horses.**

items.prompt: Why do people in a Sydney office care about a race in Melbourne?
items.answer: They stop at 3 pm to watch it together. In the sweep, everyone has a horse.

rows.example: Who did you get? I got the number 7 horse.

blocks.title: Part 4: Work Rules That Surprise Visitors
paragraphs: **No tips.** In cafés and restaurants, people do not usually leave a **tip**. A tip is a little money for the person who serves you.
Why? **Australian workers already get high pay.** So they do not need tips to make enough money.
The lowest pay the law allows is called the **minimum wage**. From 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 an hour for adults. The Fair Work Commission decides this number every year.
**Super.** Every boss must also pay **12% of a worker's pay into a super fund**. Super is short for superannuation. The fund keeps this money until you are old.
Why? **So people have their own money when they stop work.**
The rule changed on 1 July 2026. **Now the boss pays super with every payday**, the day you get your pay.
**Long service leave.** After **10 years with the same company**, workers get **long service leave**. It is a long holiday, and you still get your pay.
In New South Wales, the state where Sydney is, it is **two months**. Other states have different rules.
Why? **It is a thank-you for staying with one company for a long time.**

blocks.title: Scene: Saturday at the Lake
paragraphs: It is Saturday, 31 October, at Lake Burley Griffin in Canberra. You meet your friend Jack, who lives there. The rowing club has a sausage sizzle by the water.
Phrases to use: Do you feel like ... / How long does it take to ... / What's it for? / Keep the change.
Your goal: buy lunch at the sausage sizzle and plan the afternoon with Jack.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Hey, you made it! How's the new job in Sydney?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Good, but busy. On Tuesday my office stops at 3 pm for a horse race.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: The Melbourne Cup! Everyone watches it. Are you hungry?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Very. Something smells good.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: That's the rowing club. They're having a sausage sizzle.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What's it for?

turns.speaker: Club member
turns.text: We're raising money for a new boat.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Great. Can I get one with onions, please? And a bottle of water.

turns.speaker: Club member
turns.text: Sure. That's five fifty: three fifty for the sausage, two for the water.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Here's six dollars. Keep the change.

turns.speaker: Club member
turns.text: Thanks, mate! The sauce is on the table.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Jack, was this lake always here?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: No, it's not natural. Workers built a dam in 1963, and the river filled the lake.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Why did the people who planned the city want a lake?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: The river was in low land between hills, so water could fill it cheaply. And a lake makes the city beautiful. Do you feel like a walk after lunch?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Sure. How long does it take to walk around it?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: All of it is too far. The bridge-to-bridge loop is 5 kilometres, over two bridges. That takes about an hour.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Perfect. Do you feel like a barbecue tomorrow too?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Good idea. The barbecues by the water are free. I'll bring the sausages.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Then I'll bring the bread. Why don't we meet here at twelve?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Twelve is good. See you then.

blocks.title: Scene: Cup Day at the Office
paragraphs: It is Tuesday, 3 November, at 2:50 pm in your Sydney office. Chloe and Liam, who work with you, are in the kitchen. The Melbourne Cup starts on TV at 3 pm.
Phrases to use: Count me in. / Who did you get? / Is it true that ... / How long have you been at ...
Your goal: join the sweep, watch the race and ask about work rules in Australia.

blocks.title: Conversation: Cup Day at the Office

turns.speaker: Chloe
turns.text: There you are! We're doing a sweep. It's five dollars, and you take a horse from the hat.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Count me in. Here's five dollars.

turns.speaker: Chloe
turns.text: Thanks. Close your eyes and take one name.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I got Juja Kibo. Who did you get, Liam?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Point Of Law. It's the favourite! Most people think it will win.

turns.speaker: Chloe
turns.text: Lucky you. We have twenty people, so there's a hundred dollars. First place gets fifty, second gets thirty and third gets twenty.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Does all of Australia really stop for this?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Pretty much. In Melbourne it's a public holiday. Here we just stop work for about ten minutes.

turns.speaker: Chloe
turns.text: It's three o'clock. They're off!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Come on, Juja Kibo!

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Point Of Law is in front... Yes! Point Of Law wins!

turns.speaker: Chloe
turns.text: And Juja Kibo is third! You win twenty dollars.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Look at this. The first three horses all have the same trainer, Ciaron Maher.

turns.speaker: Chloe
turns.text: That has never happened before. It's the first time in 166 races. And the rider, Ethan Brown, won the Cup for the first time.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Liam, you won fifty dollars. Are you buying lunch?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Maybe! I want a big holiday next year. I'm taking two months off.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Two months? How long have you been at this company?

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: Ten years in March. So I get long service leave: two months, with full pay.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Is it true that the company also pays money for when we are old?

turns.speaker: Chloe
turns.text: Yes, that's super. The company pays 12% of your pay into your super fund.

turns.speaker: Liam
turns.text: And since July, it comes with every payday, not every three months.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Australian work rules are pretty good!

turns.speaker: Chloe
turns.text: Not bad, right? Okay, back to work.

blocks.title: Speaking
paragraphs: With a partner, act out Cup Day at the office again with different horses.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: Australians enjoy their free time, and their work rules look after them.

Should voting be compulsory? Why or why not?
Which Australian work rule would you like in your country?
